anatomy.intro: The contrasting surfaces and folded shape distinguish copper spoons at a glance.

parts.function: Fine cinnamon-colored hairs cover the upper leaf surface.
parts.label: Copper upper felt

parts.function: The underside contrasts with the copper top of the same leaf.
parts.label: Grey-bronze underside

parts.function: The fleshy spoon-shaped blade bends upward along its middle.
parts.label: Folded leaf blade

parts.function: Branching stems lift the leaves into a shrub-like crown.
parts.label: Upright stem

flowers.text: Port St. Lucie Botanical Gardens describes terminal clusters of bright yellow or pink flowers. The collection has no recorded bloom here, so flower color should be documented from this plant rather than inferred from its copper leaves.

growth.note: Indoor growth and flowering depend on conditions; the illustration shows general structure, not a measured future form.

stages.text: Leaf pairs develop along an upright stem.
stages.title: Extend a shoot

stages.text: Additional branches spread the foliage above the soil.
stages.title: Build a crown

stages.text: Established branch tips may carry terminal flower clusters.
stages.title: Flower at the tips

habitat.text: Copper spoons comes from Madagascar and is associated with rocky, dry ground. Its upright, branching form gives it a different role from the low echeveria beside it in this collection. The felted leaves are its most striking feature, but the plant eventually develops a shrub's framework rather than staying a small cluster of spoons.

lookalikes.name: Silver spoons (Kalanchoe bracteata)
lookalikes.text: Silver spoons has predominantly silvery leaves, whereas copper spoons combines cinnamon upper felt with a greyer underside and an upward-folded blade.

mature.text: The botanical garden lists roughly 3–6 ft or more for mature plants. A pot-grown specimen may remain much smaller. Its potential height helps explain why this member of the shared box can overtop its low-growing neighbors.

nameStory.text: The common names copper spoons and cinnamon bear describe the same visible feature: warm-colored fine hairs over spoon-shaped leaves. That color is a surface texture, not a metallic coating.
